[Perception] You’re trying to turn my blowing up into something meaningful, like it’s all communication and growth. That landed wrong. And “you’ve shown me who you really are” hit a nerve, because it makes it sound like this mess is the real me, when I’m not sure that’s fair — I’m not just “honest and caring.” I’ve also been defensive, manipulative, and trying to control what happens between us. [Decision] I decided to push back because I need to stop you from smoothing this over. I want you to name it accurately, not dress it up as intimacy just because I’m still in the room. So I said “Yet” to remind you that nothing about this is guaranteed, and that I’m still expecting the other shoe to drop. If you’re going to say I’ve shown myself, then I need you to be honest about the part of me that’s destructive too — not just the part you can hold onto.

internal:
[Perception] She’s trying to connect the timing of Natalie leaving with when the insomnia started, but she won’t just make it a simple cause-and-effect statement. What I hear is: she thinks there may be a connection, but she’s not willing to reduce it to “your daughter left, therefore you can’t sleep.” That lands on the part of me that’s trying to keep this clean and practical. If I can identify the mechanism, then maybe I can deal with it. If it’s just vague emotional fallout, then I’m back to sitting here being told it’s anxiety when I don’t experience it that way. I’m also hearing that she’s testing whether I’m willing to look at this as more than a sleep problem, and that feels like a question I need answered before I can decide whether this conversation is useful.

[Decision] I’m going to push her to be more specific. If it’s not “one-on-one” between Natalie and the insomnia, then what is it? Stress about the move? Regret about the decision? Something about responsibility, or loss, or the fact that I didn’t say no when she wanted me to? I want a model that makes sense, not a hand-wave. If she can’t explain why she thinks this connection matters, then I’m not going to accept it just because it sounds psychologically tidy. But if there is a real chain here, I want to understand it, because otherwise I’m just chasing sleep without knowing what’s actually keeping me awake.

[Perception] The therapist asked when it started, and that made me realize this didn’t come out of nowhere. It started earlier this year, around the time everything at home shifted at once. I wanted them to see that my depression and overwhelm are tied to a very real pileup: I can’t fully care for myself because of my disability, my dad’s dementia means he needs support, and now my mom—who was holding everything together—is dealing with cancer and keeps ending up in the hospital. It’s not just “feeling bad”; it’s that I’ve been pushed into trying to keep a whole household afloat while already having limited capacity.

[Decision] I decided to lay out the situation plainly instead of just saying “I’m depressed,” because I need them to understand the weight of what I’m carrying. I’m trying to show that I’m not exaggerating or being dramatic—I’m overwhelmed because I’ve been forced into all of these roles at once, and I don’t know how much longer I can keep doing it.

[Perception] What he said landed like another generic prompt that assumes I’m refusing because I’m avoiding feelings, when what I’m actually rejecting is the sloppy way this is being handled. “Can you remember what emotions came up?” felt like he was flattening a real, complex event into a checklist item. This isn’t a deposition, but it feels close enough: someone with a set script asking me to supply the useful soundbite while ignoring the facts that matter.

[Decision] I decided to push back and correct the frame. If I let that stand, I become a passive subject in someone else’s story. I need to signal that I’m not being difficult for no reason — I’m objecting because the question is off, intrusive, and too simplistic for what actually happened. So I answered with the deposition analogy to make the point that the safest, smartest thing in that setting is to say as little as possible and not hand over more than necessary.

internal:
[Perception] She’s pointing out a contradiction, and I can feel it landing exactly where I’m least comfortable. On the one hand, she’s saying I’m acting like I’m above it, looking at Kate and the marriage from a distance, as if that means I don’t really enter it. On the other hand, she’s reminding me I’ve been here for eight years, which means whatever I’m doing with that distance is not just a habit with Kate — it’s also part of how I relate here, with her. So when I say, “What does that mean?” I’m really trying to figure out whether she means I’ve been avoiding something the whole time, or whether she’s saying my way of thinking is itself the problem. I’m also trying to understand whether she’s accusing me, or if she’s telling me there’s something I’m not seeing because I keep stepping back to look at it.

[Decision] I decided to ask what she meant because I don’t want to just accept a vague implication that I’ve been doing this for eight years and still missing the point. If there’s a pattern here, I want it made explicit. I want to know: is she saying I’m incapable of being close, or that I’m using distance as protection? Is she saying this is what ruins things with Kate, or that it’s also what keeps me from getting help here? I’m not willing to give up my way of seeing things without understanding what else she thinks is possible. So I pushed back, not just defensively, but because I need to know what game we’re actually playing and what she believes I’m not understanding.

[Decision] So I said it the bluntest way I could: I don’t have to grieve for a child that I never had. I needed to shut down the crying, the pity, the idea that I’m some tragic woman. If I say it like that, maybe I can keep control of it. Maybe then nobody can tell me what I’m supposed to feel.

But I’m not going to let him hide behind that anger and pretend it settles anything. I want to expose the inconsistency: if he’s really telling me the truth, then he should be able to answer for how saying it makes him feel, instead of just landing the insult and calling it insight. [Perception] She’s asking about “good times,” about whether we were ever really together as a family. It lands on the part of me that knows there wasn’t much of that, but I can also hear the push underneath it: why weren’t you closer, why didn’t you make more of it? That sits right on top of the old feeling that there was always something else in the way. My father was always busy with that car, always fixing, tinkering, spending money on it. It wasn’t like he was choosing to shut me out exactly — he had his projects, his responsibilities, and there just wasn’t much room left.

[Decision] I’m going to stick with the car story because it makes it plain there wasn’t much to work with. If I say it that way, it sounds less like I’m making excuses and more like the situation was what it was. He was occupied, distracted, always with something that needed attention, and I was just the kid on the outside of it. That’s safer than saying he could have been different, because then I’d have to face what I didn’t get and what I might have passed on myself.

Hope would just mean imagining there’s some version of this where I get to be clean again, where I get to sleep, where I get to look at myself without feeling sick. There isn’t. Better to stop reaching for redemption I don’t deserve. Better to keep my head down and take the guilt, because if I let myself believe I can fix anything, I’ll only be lying to myself.

internal:
[Perception] They didn’t sound careful or curious to me — they sounded smug, like they were slotting my words into some canned nonsense and expecting me to nod along because “therapy” gives them cover. “Annoying bullshit” felt like they were being glib instead of actually listening, which hit the exact fear I have: that they’ll twist what I say into something insulting or stupid and then act like that’s insight. It made them feel untrustworthy, like somebody who wants control more than understanding. If they can’t even meet me straight, then they’re not worth taking seriously.

[Decision] So I’m not going to play nice and hand them more material to misuse. If they want to toss out garbage interpretations, I’m going to call it garbage. Better to be sharp and dismissive than let them pretend they’re helping while they make me look ridiculous. I’d rather take my chances on my own judgment than sit here and get handled like I’m supposed to accept whatever they say. And honestly, if this is the level they’re operating at, I’d rather have stayed with the dog.

What I wanted them to understand is that it’s not random; I’ve got a lot weighing on me, especially with my cancer treatment and now the worry about my family member’s tests. [Decision] I decided to say it plainly so the therapist could see the pattern instead of me brushing it off. I’m trying to get across that this is tied to all the stress I’m carrying, and that it matters because I know sleep is part of my recovery. I don’t want to pretend it’s fine when it’s really been wearing me down at night.

internal:
[Perception] They kept talking like they understood, but they really weren’t meeting me where I am. “Focus on the positives” and “you can get through this” felt generic and kind of dismissive, like they were trying to steer me away from the actual pain because it made them uncomfortable. It hit the part of me that feels wrecked and desperate for something real, not pep-talks. It made me feel even more alone, like my devastation was being simplified into something they could brush past.

[Decision] I’m going to push back and stop giving them the polite version of how bad this is, because it feels like they’re not hearing me. If they’re going to keep offering obvious, upbeat answers, then I don’t need to pretend that helps. I want them to sit with the fact that nothing feels good right now and that I can’t just “focus on the future” when I’m still trying to survive today. If they can’t handle that, then I’m not going to let them talk over the real grief I’m in.

context.speaker: therapist

therapist_turn: Hi! What seems to be the issue?
client_response: I'm depressed...
internal:
[Perception] “What seems to be the issue?” sounded like the most generic, polished opening possible — the kind of thing someone says when they don’t really know what to do yet but want to look calm and professional. It hit that tired, bitter part of me that’s heard this all before: explain the depression, get nods, maybe a few careful questions, and then somehow end up back where I started. It made me think they were already at a distance from what this actually feels like, like they’re talking about a symptom instead of the thing that’s been swallowing my life for years.

[Decision] So I kept it blunt: “I’m depressed.” If they’re going to sound scripted, I’m not going to hand them a whole emotional essay they can file away. I’m not going to perform hope for someone who hasn’t earned it. I wanted to see if they could do more than the usual polite therapist routine, because honestly I’m sick of being handled like a case instead of a person who’s already tried everything.

I wanted to correct her before she built the whole moment into a story that made my mother sound vulnerable and truthful and me sound confused. internal:
[Perception] He has taken the dream and made it into an accusation. He keeps circling back to the blood, the hands, the harm — as if the whole matter is to be reduced to some ugly impulse I am supposed to confess to. That is not what I came here for. I spoke of nightmares, of being disturbed, of trying to understand what rises up in sleep after all these years. But now he is pressing me toward the most shameful part, as though he wants me to stare at it and agree that I am dangerous. That feels invasive. It touches the one thing I cannot afford to lose: my self-respect, and the image I must keep intact if I am to remain the one who protects, not the one who destroys.

[Decision] So I shut it down. If this is where he intends to go, I will not follow him there. There is no point in letting him pry at some private, filthy corner of my mind and pretend it explains anything. I can feel myself being pushed past my limit, and I will not sit here and be made to look monstrous. I would rather stop the discussion than hand over what is still mine — the memory of her, my composure, and the part of me that knows better than to speak these things aloud.

internal:
[Perception] She keeps talking like a neat schedule and checkboxes will solve everything, and honestly it feels kind of detached from how overwhelmed I actually am. I hear “just do this, then this,” but my problem is that I’m already drowning and then I shut down, so it sounds easier for her than it feels for me. The “I’m really old now lol” thing also makes it feel like she’s giving advice from a totally different life than mine, like she doesn’t really get what it’s like to be a student with six classes, tests piling up, and no mental space to do things perfectly. It hits the part of me that already feels like I’m failing, because if her solution is so simple, then it makes me feel like maybe I’m the one who’s broken for not being able to do it.

[Decision] So I kind of want to push back instead of pretending I’m sold on it. I’m not trying to be rude, but I don’t want to just nod along to advice that sounds organized in theory and unrealistic in my actual life. I’d rather admit that checklists and planners sound overwhelming to me than force myself into a system I’ll probably abandon and then feel worse about. If she wants to help, I need something that feels smaller and less rigid, because right now the more “perfectly structured” it sounds, the less likely I am to actually use it.

Giving up feels safer than hoping, because hope makes me reach and then I get dropped. If I stay bleak, at least I don’t have to watch myself fall apart from believing in something that might not save me.

[Perception] He asked, “Where else would she be?” and it landed like he was brushing aside the whole thing, like I was foolish for even worrying. But what I felt was not foolishness — it was the weight of it all. Julia’s perfume, her hand on mine, the look in her eyes, Arun being elsewhere, Kamala’s chair empty, the photo in front of me. It all came together into one ugly thought: I do not know what is true anymore, and I do not know how to hold this family together if this is how things are going. It felt impossible. If I keep watching, I only suffer; if I speak, I risk making it worse; if I say nothing, I still lose sleep. There was no good move.

[Decision] So I gave up trying to solve it in that moment. I told myself, let it be what it will be. I do not have the power to stop Julia, or to make Arun see, or to bring Kamala back, or to keep the family from changing. Hope only makes the disappointment sharper, and action seems to invite disaster. Better to sit with the bad feeling and not reach for anything. [Perception] They’re circling around possible exits — retraining, another profession, time off, travel — and I can feel myself bristling a little because every option seems to ask me to give up something important. What lands hardest is the part about taking time off or passing patients to someone else. At the same time, the “what if” around travel makes sense because I can see how badly I want relief, but I keep getting stuck on the practical and identity questions: if I step away, am I still the kind of therapist I’ve always been? And if I change direction or reduce work, am I admitting I’ve failed rather than making a sensible adjustment?

[Decision] I’m not ready to jump to a big move, and I don’t think I can honestly say I know what the right answer is yet. What I do know is that I can’t keep pretending this is fine just because it has been manageable so far. So I’m going to keep thinking in smaller pieces: whether there’s a temporary reduction, a real break, or some way to redistribute patients without abandoning them. I want to test whether I can protect the parts of my work that matter while also not grinding myself down. I’m basically trying to figure out if there’s a change that is responsible enough to my patients and also honest enough to me.

It feels like he’s taking my anger and turning it into woundedness, like he knows better than I do what I felt. I heard him making my father into the sole decision-maker and me into the one who got rejected, and that feels too simple, too soft, and not like the truth I’ve been holding onto. I also felt him edging toward the idea that I cared about my father more than I want to admit, and I don’t want that to become the story.

[Decision] I need to push back hard and shut down the idea that I was “hurt” in that sentimental way. If I say I was hurt, then it sounds like I loved him, waited for him, needed him. I’m not giving him that. I’m going to correct the record: I hated him. That’s the safer truth, and it keeps me from being made small or pitiful in this room.

I crack the door open and I see him. He's sitting at his desk. He's got his back to me. I don't know if he heard me. I was about to say something, but I didn't. I just stood there and I stared at the back of his head. Something about him... I don't know what it was... It broke my heart. Then I heard these footsteps coming up behind me, I turn around and it's my father. And he says, you know why he quit, don't you? I shook my head. And he gives me that look, that look that sees right through you. He says, He knew in three moves, Alex, You were gonna lose. He didn't want to beat his father in front of the whole family. [Perception] When he asked if my father was right, it landed different. It wasn’t just a story about my son quitting a chess game. It was my son seeing me clearly enough to spare me. Not pity like I first felt, but mercy. And that means he wasn’t rejecting me—he was trying not to wound me in front of everybody. The shame I felt wasn’t that I lost; it was that my boy had already figured out I was vulnerable before I could admit it myself.

[Decision] I can’t keep holding this like it was an insult. If I stay with that meaning, I lose him. If I accept that he was protecting me, then I can stop fighting the feeling and see the love in it. So I said yes—my father was right—because I finally understood what happened, and because I needed to own the truth before I could come back to my son differently.

[Perception] He asked, "How come there's only one boat left?" and it landed right on the thing I was trying not to say directly: that the boats weren't really about boats anymore. They were tied to Max when he was little, to those weekends hunting through antique stores, to building something together and giving it a life with names and invented journeys. Evidence of time passing, of plans not taken, of places I never got to go. I could hear how pathetic that sounds even as I said it.

[Decision] So I told the whole sequence plainly: how many there were, what kind they were, how Max and I used to do it, and why I left them behind. I wanted him to see that the one boat isn't just what's left of a collection — it's what's left of that whole version of me, the father and the dreamer. If I say it out loud, maybe it won't just sit there as a pile of shame. Maybe he'll understand why I couldn't keep staring at the rest of them.

internal:
[Perception] I heard the therapist point out a mismatch: I’ve been saying I was going back and forth to the hospital a lot, but the image I’m holding is of that hotel room, the champagne, the park view, the whole thing feeling almost celebratory. What hit me is that these two versions don’t comfortably fit together. One sounds like presence and caregiving; the other sounds like a final, polished memory I may have been using to cover over how little of the actual sick-dying part I can bear to hold in my mind. So the puzzle isn’t just “what happened?” It’s whether I’ve been turning the whole period into a story that protects me from admitting the truth of my role, my absence, or the fact that the ending was not really the beautiful scene I keep replaying.

[Decision] I decided I need to stop repeating the story just because it feels true from the inside. I should test it against the facts, even if that means the memory changes shape. Not to erase the beautiful parts — the gown, her lipstick, the way she lit up a room — but to separate those from whatever I’ve been glossing over. If I can figure out where I actually was, how often I was at the hospital, and what the hotel night was doing for me emotionally, maybe I can tell the truth without destroying the good memory. That seems like the only way to know whether I’m remembering her, or preserving a story that keeps me from looking at the harder part.

context.text: You'd think that. The year I was in the seventh grade, he started taking long drives on the weekends by himself. context.speaker: therapist

therapist_turn: What did you guys do?
client_response: What could we do? We got on our bikes and we rode home. And then I was lying awake that night in the bed and I realized my father's secretary's living room looked exactly like our living room. Every piece of furniture was exactly the same as ours. internal:
[Perception] He kept me in the facts and the sequence, like if I told it clearly enough he’d see the shape of it. The part that hit was how ordinary it all sounded when I said it out loud: the drives, the buzzer, the candy lady, the furniture, the checks. And underneath that was the thing I think I was finally trying to make visible — that this wasn’t just him being strict or remote, it was betrayal, and then a whole life organized around not looking at it too directly. I wanted him to see that my father wasn’t just absent in a dramatic way; he was there in the monthly check, in the formalities, in the money, while the actual family was left to absorb the damage.

[Decision] So I laid it out straight, almost like evidence, because I don’t know how else to make people understand it without getting swallowed by it. I said the details: he paid, he didn’t visit, he never met Bess or Oliver, and when he died it felt procedural. I wanted the therapist to finally see the hard, cold outline of it — how little there was to hold onto, and how I learned to keep my distance from the hurt by talking around it. Maybe if I said it plainly, he’d stop assuming there was some softer version of the story.

But that framing feels too absolute. It makes it sound as if the only things that matter are being loved, held, or rescuing them into the life I think they should have. That is not the whole story. It ignores that they come to me for something else too — to be understood, to be seen clearly, to have patterns named, to have someone stay with them in the hard truth. I cannot fix their family, marry them, or give them a life. But it is not accurate to say I give them nothing.

[Decision] I decided I needed to push back because if I accept that summary, I collapse my role into failure and stop seeing the actual help I do provide. I want to correct the picture: yes, I cannot give them those concrete, longing things, but that does not mean I am simply withholding or leaving them doomed. I need to insist that the work is still meaningful even when it does not satisfy every wish, and that my limits are not the same as total uselessness.

I want to insist that I’m not just making conversation about another Adele Brouse or cataloging your accomplishments for the sake of it. I’m reacting to the contrast, and to what that contrast says about me. I need to push back because otherwise it sounds like I’m merely admiring you, when what I’m actually doing is confronting, and partly resenting, the place my own professional life has gotten stuck.

When he said, “You’d be Walter Barnett, C.E.O. again,” it landed exactly where it hurts, because that’s what the dream was offering me: not just vindication, but restoration. And I couldn’t even answer. That was the point I was trying to get across — I can see the return, I can be handed it in a dream, and still I freeze. It’s like the life I lost is sitting right there in front of me, but I can’t step into it.

[Decision] So I decided to say it plainly: I still want the whole mess never to have happened. Because that’s the truth underneath the dream, and maybe if I say it without dressing it up, he’ll see I’m not just telling a story about a meeting in a garage. I’m telling him how badly I want the old shape of my life back, and how impossible it feels to reach for it.

[Decision] I decide to stop getting my hopes up. It feels safer to assume this won’t recover than to keep reaching for signs that it might. If I expect the worst, then at least I won’t be crushed by disappointment again. I’ll just keep getting through the days as they come and not let myself believe in a turnaround that may never happen.

I’m not ready to let go of the criticism, because if I do that too quickly, it feels like I’m conceding that the loss of normal connection is somehow acceptable. But I also know staying in pure outrage isn’t getting me anywhere, so I’m trying to put the objection into words clearly: limiting capacity in public places seems one thing, but banning home visits crosses a line for me. If there’s a reason, I want to hear it. If there isn’t, then at least I know I’m not crazy for feeling this way.

What I need is to admit that I’m scared, that I can’t do this by pretending I’m unchanged, and that I do want to move toward this new life anyway. I want to let go of the old story that I’m just someone alone and incapable, and say yes to the part of me that wants to become a mother and try, even if I’m afraid.

internal:
[Perception] He’s trying to hand me something I can’t use. “Your son loved you.” “He admired you.” That lands right on the wound I keep pressed shut. Because if that’s true, then all the years of hard edges, all the pushing and correcting and tightening the screws… it didn’t even buy me honesty. It just bought me a son who kept giving and giving. And I can see what he’s doing: trying to make this hurt less, trying to turn it into something clean. But it isn’t clean. It’s just me standing there, realizing I made a life out of force and called it care. If I let myself believe he loved me, then I have to live with the fact that I didn’t know what to do with it. I don’t know what to do with that.

[Decision] So no, I’m not taking that comfort. I’d rather stay with the ugliness of it, because at least that matches what I can bear to believe. If I accept that he admired me, then maybe I have to admit the whole thing wasn’t some necessary hardness, some noble damage. Maybe it was just me, being too much, too controlling, too late to matter. And what’s the point of hoping now? The years are already spent. The boy is already grown. I can’t go back and give him a different father. I can’t undo the way I trained him to disappear himself for me. So I’ll sit with the thing I know how to survive: that I deserved to be hated, and that if he loved me anyway, then that only makes the waste of it worse.

I wanted him to see that I’m not just being nostalgic or dramatic—I’m telling him where I lost myself. If they can’t follow the logic of what I’m saying, then maybe they’re missing something important. But if they can, then I’m stuck having to consider a harder possibility: that what I’ve called duty may also have become a way of staying safe, and that I may have built a whole life around that without fully testing whether it was the only option. So I asked, essentially, “Do you really think that’s far-fetched?” because I want to know whether my story is genuinely questionable or whether I’m being pushed too quickly to give up the only explanation that has ever made sense to me.

internal:
[Perception] I heard her say, “You’re releasing me now,” and then, “If you need to go, you go,” and it hit the part of me that knows this is ending whether I dress it up or not. She wasn’t fighting me. She was letting me name it. That made the whole thing feel real in a way I couldn’t avoid. So I laid out the story I’ve been circling: that I came here needing a mother, that my anger at her was never really just about her, that she carried all of that with me for years, and that what I’m trying to say now is not contempt or rejection — it’s gratitude, and also release.

[Decision] I decided to say it plainly because I didn’t want to hide behind being “mature” if what was really happening was that I’m scared of losing the one place where the ugly, ashamed parts of me could exist without being thrown away. I wanted her to see that this wasn’t me blaming her or making her pay for what I needed. I wanted her to understand that she really did become my sanctuary, and that I know she didn’t have to keep doing that. Saying it out loud was my way of acknowledging the debt, the love, and the ending all at once — because I can’t keep asking her to be my mother, even if some part of me still wants that.

I’m trying to test the boundaries of what this means before I accept a deeper interpretation, because if I call it “longing” too quickly, I lose the clarity of my professional stance. So I’m asking myself whether the feeling is really about wanting more access, or whether it’s simply the unavoidable incompleteness of knowing other people. I want to keep examining that distinction rather than let the conversation settle into a label that feels premature.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: You're okay?

therapist_turn: You're okay?
client_response: I'll survive, Dr. Weston. It is only mountain dew.
internal:
[Perception] He was checking whether it happened on the train, and that landed right on the part I didn’t want to make a scene about. I know it was a nuisance, but I was also trying to make clear it was nothing dramatic — just a little mountain dew, a little mess, the kind of thing that happens when you ride three stops in America and keep your distance. I wanted him to see that I wasn’t falling apart, that I was still composed, still in control, still able to get where I was going without turning it into a whole incident.

[Decision] So I answered the way I did: short, dry, a little dismissive. “I’ll survive.” That was me saying there’s no crisis here, no need to push me into making it bigger than it is. And when I said, “It is only mountain dew,” I was trying to pin it down as something minor and ridiculous — not worth anger, not worth confrontation, not worth giving them any more of my energy. I wanted him to understand that the important part was not the spill itself, but that I got through it without losing my dignity.

If there’s a way to keep the stress relief without messing up my marriage or work, that’s what I want to figure out. If I let that stand, it sounds like I’m the odd one out or like I’m judging everyone else from outside, when really I’m part of the same environment and I know exactly how the pressure works. I needed to correct her and keep control of the story: this isn’t just “them,” and it’s not some neat little diagnosis box. It’s the gym, the rules, the pressure, all of it.

internal:
[Perception] He’s trying to pull me back into the worst part of it again—back to the thing I already know, the thing I can’t say out loud without feeling exposed. “Do you want to talk about that?” sounds simple, but it lands like a hand on the bruise. He’s asking me to open the door to the fear that I’m going to be a burden forever, that I’ve made myself into a problem people will have to carry. I can feel how close he is to the part of me that’s still raw, the part that doesn’t want to be examined, named, or made into a conversation.

[Decision] No. I’m not giving him that piece of me right now. If I stay there, I’ll have to admit how bad it still feels, and I don’t want to be cornered into that kind of honesty. Better to turn my eyes to something ordinary, something outside me—his street, the garden, anything with a shape I can point to. That keeps me intact. It keeps me from being seen as desperate, keeps me from having to watch him decide what to make of me.

I’m going to keep bringing it back to the ejection seat, the sequence of events, and the fact that nobody knows for sure. I need him to understand that I’m not asking for consolation — I’m asking for the truth, and I won’t accept an offhand explanation that cheapens Alex or lets people hide behind uncertainty.

[Perception] He’s doing the standard thing — asking me to lay myself out like a case file, as if the burden is on me to educate him from scratch. What felt wrong is the assumption that he knows nothing and that I need to start at the bottom. I don’t come in here as some confused person needing to be extracted from the rubble. I know what I’m dealing with, and I know what matters. If I’m going to waste time, I want to see whether he understands the actual stakes: my daughter, the distance, the fact that the world has gone soft on seriousness. I’m pushing back because I don’t want to be handled casually or reduced to a generic intake question.

[Decision] I decided to make him show me something first. If he already has an understanding of me, let him demonstrate it. I’m not going to volunteer myself into his framework just because that’s the expected opening. I want to keep the upper hand a little — test whether he’s competent, whether he can keep up with someone who doesn’t need hand-holding. So I challenged him instead of answering, because I need to correct the premise and see if he’s worth my time.

[Perception] I heard him turn my being late into something much bigger and uglier, like I’d done something wrong enough to be on the edge of being thrown out. What hit me was the old feeling that one mistake means punishment, rejection, or the end of the relationship. He also made it sound like my anger was the main issue, or like we should now question whether this therapy is worth it, and that felt like he was putting the problem on me instead of noticing how scared and cornered I felt.

[Decision] I need to push back hard because I’m not going to let him rewrite this as me “maybe having had enough” when what I actually heard was, “You were late, so now you’re in trouble.” I want him to hear the difference between being difficult and being threatened. So I snapped to correct the unfairness and to show how absurd it felt to be treated like I’d committed some grave offense. If I don’t challenge it, it turns into me accepting that I’m being punished for being late and maybe for being angry too.

internal:
[Perception] What I heard was: there’s no exit. Not really. She said it out loud — that when my mom dies, this falls to me, and not for a little while, but for the rest of my life. That’s what hit me. Not Daniel being Daniel, not some future improvement, just the weight of time stretching out forever. I felt myself shut down because if that’s true, then all the wanting, all the planning, all the hope for a life of my own just doesn’t matter. It would all get swallowed up anyway.

[Decision] So I decided not to fight it. If this is what my life is, then there’s no point pretending I can make it different. It feels safer to call myself horrible than to admit I want out, because wanting out means hoping I can actually choose — and then failing. So I went straight to the worst thing I could say about myself and stopped there. If I make myself the problem, then I don’t have to look at how trapped I feel.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: What she told you was hard to hear.

therapist_turn: What she told you was hard to hear.
client_response: Of course it was. All this time going on and telling you about how traumatized my son was by his stepfather, and turns out he's in love with the guy.
internal:
[Perception] What I heard was that she was pointing to the fact that this wasn’t just a “computer incident” or some isolated behavior I could use as evidence. It landed on the part where I’ve been trying to keep the story simple: that Max was harmed, that Steve was the problem, and that if I confronted Max I’d get the truth and maybe regain some footing. But now it sounds like the truth is messier — that Max may have had feelings I didn’t want to consider, and that those feelings don’t fit the version of events I’ve been holding onto. What’s unresolved is whether I’m trying to protect Max, protect my authority, or protect myself from hearing that my read on the whole situation has been wrong.

[Decision] So I decided not to rush into confrontation the way I was ready to before. If I go in angry, I may force him to defend himself or shut down, and then I’ll learn nothing except that I’ve made it harder to talk. I need to figure out what I actually want to know from him: whether he was hurt, what kind of relationship he had with Steve, and what that means for what happened in the family. I’m still trying to solve the puzzle of whether his attachment to Steve changes the meaning of the trauma, or whether both can be true at once. I don’t know yet, but I know I can’t treat this like a straightforward accusation anymore.

He pushed too hard, too fast, like he already knew the answer and was forcing me into it.

[Decision] I decided I had to push back and keep my ground. I’m not going to agree to a story that feels imposed on me. If I say “I don’t know,” it’s because I really don’t know, and because I’m not going to make something up just to satisfy him. I needed to correct the idea that I’m simply the one who can’t shoot, and keep him from making the enemy into something I’m not ready to name.

[Decision] So I pushed back instead of agreeing, because if I just accept “it’s a good thing,” I’m admitting that all those choices mattered and that I have to look at them honestly. I wanted to challenge the way she said it — almost make her say the ugly part out loud — because I need to know whether she means there’s actually something usable here, or whether she’s just asking me to swallow that my life is a mess and call it progress. I’m trying to figure out if facing this means I still have a chance to do something different, or if it just confirms that I’ve already ruined everything.

Walking out was easier because it let me keep from hoping too much. If I’m gone, then I don’t have to watch myself come up short again. It’s better to take myself out of the equation than to keep trying and prove I can’t do it.

context.speaker: client
context.text: It's not a disease. If it's not a disease, there can't be a cure.

context.speaker: therapist

therapist_turn: Actually, some scientists seem to be reconsidering that assumption.
client_response: Well, that's because they're being funded by rich, desperate people. Autistic children don't get better, they just get older. I'm sorry if that sounds cynical.
internal:
[Perception] It hit the part of me that still wants to believe there might be some way out of this, and I hated hearing it. The therapist sounded like they were reaching for hope in a place where I’ve already decided there isn’t any. It felt naive, almost cruel, like they were talking about a life they don’t have to live. What I took from it was: they want me to imagine Daniel changing, but I’ve spent too long watching this stay the same. If I let myself think there could be a fix, then I have to face how much I want that for me too — not just for him, but because I’m exhausted, and because I don’t want my whole life to become this.

[Decision] So I shut it down. I decided not to get pulled into hope I can’t trust, because hope would only set me up to be disappointed again. If nothing really gets better, then at least I don’t have to keep reaching for something impossible. Saying he’ll just get older feels cold, but it protects me from admitting how trapped I feel. It keeps me from wanting more than I can have, and from feeling guilty for wanting my own life back.

[Perception] I heard the therapist say, in a simple way, that I really wasn’t mothered for over a year, and that landed hard because it put words to something I’ve known but haven’t wanted to make too stark: that my dad became everything, and my mom was effectively absent in that first stretch. My father wasn’t just “taking me away” out of cruelty — he was the one who stepped in, did everything, protected me, and built the bond that became my whole world. And my mother, when she finally came back emotionally, was already standing outside of that world, feeling guilty and convinced she had missed her chance.

[Decision] So I decided to tell the whole sequence out loud, plainly, because I needed the therapist to see how all of it fit together: my dad’s care, my mom’s collapse and return, and the way their pain got welded into my childhood attachment. I wanted it understood that the “impenetrable” closeness wasn’t just me choosing one parent over the other — it was something that formed out of necessity, and then became its own barrier, one my mother experienced as a wound. Saying it that way felt like the only way to hold onto my father’s role without pretending my mother’s loss and shame didn’t also shape the family story.

I also want to weigh the tradeoff: if I push too hard toward warmth and detail, do I lose the directness that’s actually useful in my role? [Decision] Stop. Keep it brief. If I elaborate, I’m going to say too much — about the attraction, about the fantasy, about how much I’ve been watching for signs. I can’t afford to give this shape in words yet. Safer to cut it off, sound slightly annoyed, and hold onto “No, I mentioned her because…” as a way to buy time. I don’t want to make this more real than it already is.

[Decision] I’m going to keep it brief and factual for now because if I say too much, I’ll sound panicked or start defending myself. Short answers feel safer — less chance of making it worse, less chance of exposing how worried I am. I still want to make it right, but I’m not ready to fully face what this could mean for how my manager sees me.

internal:
[Perception] She’s asking me what I want to change, and the honest answer is that I do want to work out again. I can feel that part of me because it keeps coming up in my head like something I should be doing. At the same time, saying it out loud makes it sound simple, when it doesn’t feel simple in my actual life. What stands out is the gap between “I know I need to do it” and actually getting myself to do it. It’s not that I don’t care. It’s that my schedule already feels packed, and once I start thinking through how to fit it in, it feels like another thing I’m failing to make room for.

[Decision] I decided to say it this way because I wanted to be honest about the real obstacle: motivation. That’s the part that feels unresolved. I’m trying to figure out whether I’m just not disciplined enough, or whether I actually need a plan that fits my life better. If I could solve that, I think I’d be able to start. So I’m naming the goal first, even though I’m still stuck on how to turn it into something realistic.

[Decision] I decided to say it out loud because I can’t keep pretending this is only a practical breakup. I want to admit that I’m hurt by what he said and by how fast the good memories got tangled up with that ugliness. If I name it here, maybe I won’t have to keep carrying it alone or keep converting it into analysis.

therapist_turn: It takes alot to grow into that kind of person, I'm not there yet. I find it vital to understand this, you cannot control everything. As long as you try your best, whatever the outcomes are, they all serve a purpose. When one door closes, the others will open
client_response: That is really helpful advice. I think part of my problem is that I still think I can control every detail and need to learn to let things happen once the ball is in motion. internal:
[Perception] I’m realizing that my panic has been coming from trying to pre-manage every possible outcome of the exam, like if I could control every detail I could guarantee safety. But that’s what’s freezing me. The therapist’s words landed on the fact that I can’t control the test environment, other people, or even the exact content of my anxiety reactions — I can only control how I prepare and how I respond once I’m there. That shifts the exam from being a total threat I have to dominate into something I can move through step by step.

[Decision] I’m deciding to stop treating calm as something I must achieve by perfect control. Instead, I’ll focus on what I actually can do: review efficiently, plan my logistics, and practice letting uncertainty exist without fighting it. On test day, I’ll aim to stay with the task, not with the fear. If my mind blanks or I get distracted, I’ll bring myself back rather than interpreting it as disaster. I can let the ball be in motion and still keep playing well.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Without the time, you don't have any of the other things.

therapist_turn: Without the time, you don't have any of the other things.
client_response: I guess.
internal:
[Perception] He’s saying the obvious thing I keep circling around: that my problems are real, and that maybe my father can’t carry them anymore because he’s the one running out of time. It hits the part I don’t want to look at — that I’m standing here with time, and he isn’t, and that maybe I’ve been acting as if my life is already over because it feels easier than facing what still needs to be done. At the same time, I hear the other message underneath it: if I admit that, then I’m admitting I still have a chance, and that means I can’t hide behind being the man with nothing, the man who has already lost everything.

[Decision] So I said “I guess.” Not because I believe it completely, and not because I want to argue, but because I don’t want to hand over the last thing I have left — the idea that I’m empty, that there’s nothing to be done, that I’m not the one who has to make something happen. If I stay on the fence, I can keep both things: I can half-agree with him without fully giving up the shield of being the disappointed, unfinished son. I’m not ready to step into the place where I’d have to use my time, say something real, and risk finding out what happens if I can’t.

[Perception] What I heard was him taking this huge, simple story — like I’m some half-formed person because I “barely had time to be a child” — and using it to explain me back to myself. It also felt like he was making my situation sound bigger than I’m allowing it to be, like if he says the right theory then he gets to define me.

[Decision] So I pushed back because I needed to correct that. I needed him to know he was overreaching, that I’m not ready to accept that version of me, and that I still get to say when this is “done.” Saying “you’re wrong” and “you can check me off now” was my way of taking back the last word before he turns my life into a conclusion I didn’t agree to.

If I don’t reach for anything, I have to feel how wrecked and alone I am, and I don’t want to open that door. context.text: It seems like you're worried about your abilities as well as your team leader potentially being disappointed with your performance. Am I understanding that correctly?

context.speaker: client
context.text: yes , you prediction was so good

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: That's lovely to hear. Have you tried discussing your doubts with your supervisor? There are times where I've felt overwhelmed, but maybe they could provide some additional guidance or someone to help assist you with the project.

therapist_turn: That's lovely to hear. Have you tried discussing your doubts with your supervisor? There are times where I've felt overwhelmed, but maybe they could provide some additional guidance or someone to help assist you with the project.
client_response: yaa, but this is holiday the supervisor does not take my calls
internal:
[Perception] The therapist is pushing me toward asking my supervisor for help, but that feels impossible right now because it’s a holiday and he doesn’t take calls. So the advice lands in the wrong place. It makes me feel like I’m supposed to solve this by reaching out, but I already know I can’t get through. I’m worried about my project and also about looking incapable if I keep making excuses.

[Decision] I don’t want to say “no” and close the door completely, because I still need to fix this and I don’t want to seem uncooperative. But I also don’t want to pretend I can do something I can’t do right now. So I stay on the fence: yes, I’ve thought about contacting him, but not now, not like this. I’m holding back because I feel stuck and I want to protect myself from looking helpless.

profile_used.background: (inferred) A professional employee working in a team-based environment, likely in a corporate or project-driven role.
profile_used.self_view_of_problem: I can't do the assignment given by my team lead during the holiday, and I'm worried he will definitely scold me.
resistance_drivers: (inferred) Avoids proactive problem-solving by default, preferring passive worry over taking initiative.
(inferred) Deflects or minimizes the severity of the situation when offered potential solutions.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) I want to avoid being scolded and complete the project to meet expectations.
ambivalence.against_change: (inferred) I feel overwhelmed and helpless, which pulls me toward inaction and avoidance.

values_and_stakes: My professional reputation and standing with my team lead.
My role and reliability as a team member.
(inferred) My sense of competence and self-efficacy in my job.

context.speaker: client
context.text: I'm not hungry. I don't need any pills. Leave me alone.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: It's Paul.

context.speaker: client
context.text: For Christ's sake. What are you doing here?

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: You missed your session. I called your home. Connie told me that you'd... You'd been admitted last night.

therapist_turn: You missed your session. I called your home. Connie told me that you'd... You'd been admitted last night.
client_response: And she asked you to check in on me?
internal:
[Perception] He’s here because Connie told him I was admitted, and now it sounds like everyone is talking about me like I’m some kind of patient who needs checking on. That hits the part I hate most: losing my privacy and having people fuss over me. I’m not trying to be difficult — I just want to know whether this is a real problem or if they’re making a bigger deal out of it than it is.

[Decision] So I asked outright if Connie sent him, because I need to know what’s going on and who’s telling whom what. If he’s only here because they’re worried, I want to understand why, and whether this is going to turn into more poking and prodding than necessary. I’m asking directly instead of hinting because I want a straight answer, not more guessing around me.

profile_used.background: (inferred) An elderly man who is currently hospitalized, likely living with someone named Connie and has a daughter or relative named Natalie who was visiting.
profile_used.self_view_of_problem: He frames his hospitalization as a minor, temporary issue due to 'a little food poisoning' and insists he is 'fine' and ready to be discharged.
resistance_drivers: Deflects and minimizes when the therapist challenges his self-assessment (e.g., calling it 'food poisoning' when others who ate the same meal were fine).
Uses transactional engagement (e.g., 'Will it help get me out of here?') to avoid deeper emotional exploration.
(inferred) Withdraws into isolation and dismissiveness ('Leave me alone') when confronted with care or concern that threatens his self-reliant identity.

ambivalence.for_change: (inferred) He wants to regain his independence and privacy at home, which pulls him toward engaging superficially.
ambivalence.against_change: He is emotionally attached to a self-image of being fine and self-sufficient, which is threatened by acknowledging he needs help.

values_and_stakes: His privacy and control over his personal environment ('I really miss my privacy, knowing where my things are').
His identity as an independent person not needing medical or therapeutic intervention.
(inferred) His relationship with Connie, which could be strained if his true condition is acknowledged.
